ety.text: From the phrase jobbe of work (“piece of work”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from a variant of Middle English gobbe (“mass, lump”); or perhaps related to Middle English jobben (“to jab, thrust, peck”), or Middle English choppe (“piece, bargain”). More at gob, jab, chop.
Imitative.

senses.d: A task.
ex: I've got a job for you: could you wash the dishes?
I didn't speak to many coworkers for the ﬁrst year on the job.

senses.d: An economic role for which a person is paid.
ex: That surgeon has a great job.
He's been out of a job since being made redundant in January.

senses.d: Plastic surgery.
A sex act.
A task, or series of tasks, carried out in batch mode (especially on a mainframe computer).
A public transaction done for private profit; something performed ostensibly as a part of official duty, but really for private gain; a corrupt official business.
A robbery or heist.
Any affair or event which affects one, whether fortunately or unfortunately.
A thing or whatsit (often used in a vague way to refer to something whose name one cannot recall).
ex: Pass me that little job with the screw thread on it.
syn: Sorted by number of Google hits

senses.d: The police as a profession, act of policing, or an individual police officer.
ex: “He was ex-job, Beavis. Detective sergeant out of County, Banbury, retired in ‘59.”
“I’m job, DS Townsend. I have to report a missing person.”

senses.d: To do odd jobs or occasional work for hire.
ex: Authors of all work, to job for the season.

senses.d: To work as a jobber.
To take the loss, usually in a demeaning or submissive manner.
To buy and sell for profit, as securities; to speculate in.
To subcontract a project or delivery in small portions to a number of contractors.
ex: We wanted to sell a turnkey plant, but they jobbed out the contract to small firms.

senses.d: To seek private gain under pretence of public service; to turn public matters to private advantage.
ex: And judges job, and bishops bite the town.

senses.d: To hire or let in periods of service.
ex: […] ...and a pair of handsome horses were jobbed, with which Jos drove about in state in the park...

senses.d: To peck (of a bird); (more generally) to poke or prod (at, into).
ex: a raven pitch'd upon him, and there sate, jobbing of the sore

senses.d: To pierce or poke (someone or something), typically with a sharp or pointed object; to stab.
ex: He had ‘jobbed out’ the eye of one gentleman.

senses.d: To hit (someone) with a quick, sharp punch; to jab.
ex: A stranger jobbed me in the mug so hard that I fell off my chair.

senses.d: A sudden thrust or stab; a jab or punch.
ex: Fair dinkum, a man ought to give you a job in the b— face.

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese serviço, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin servitium (“slavery; servitude”) (compare Italian servizio, French service, Norman sèrvice, Spanish servicio), from servus (“serf”). By surface analysis, servo + -iço.
Deverbal from employer. Akin to Italian impiego, Occitan emplec, and Spanish empleo.
